speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: DISTRIBUTION BETWEEN NAVY AND AIR FORCE
speechtext:
In view of the representations which I have received with regard to prize money, and which I have brought to the attention of the Minister of National Defence, will the minister elaborate on the statement he made in this house on February 4 in answer to a question asked by the hon. member for Kamloops (Mr. Fulton)?
Hon. Brooke Claxton (Minister of National
Defence): This matter has been brought to my attention by the hon. member for Gaspe, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), the hon. member for Kamloops, and several others. In view of the widespread

interest in the question, with the leave of the house I should like to make a statement on it, supplementing the previous statements in the press and to this house.
Prize money is the term used for the old naval custom whereby the officers and men of the Royal Navy and privateers had their pay supplemented by grants out of the money received from the sale of captured enemy merchant ships. Part of this money was kept in the exchequer, and part was paid by the crown to the crews directly concerned. It should be emphasized that no one had a right to payment, but that payment was made as an act of grace. Formerly this was done by the king himself under the royal prerogative.
In modern war it has become increasingly difficult and increasingly unfair to allocate prize money to individual officers and men taking part in the capture of the prize. Consequently in the first great war officers and men of the Royal Navy shared according to to their rank and the amount of time they had spent at sea. Personnel of the Royal Canadian Navy shared in this allocation tnade by the British parliament as if they had been members of the Royal Navy. The scale operated so that an admiral, commander in chief, got 283 times as much as an ordinary seaman.
In the second world war it had become still more difficult to apportion prizes because of the part played in each capture by large numbers of ships and planes, frequently including ships and personnel of several different nations. An agreement was therefore made under which the countries of the commonwealth would share in the proceeds of the prizes taken in proportion to the peak strength each of them had had in the navies and air forces engaged on naval operations.
There is no law or custom under which any individual has any right to any part of this money.
In the United Kingdom it has been decided that one-third of the United Kingdom's share would be kept by the crown and that the remaining two-thirds would be divided between the Royal Navy and Royal Air Force in proportion to the peak strength of these two services engaged on naval operations. The navy's share will be paid to the officers and men having more than six months' service at sea on a graduated scale, which provides for the payment of ten times as much to senior officers as to men. It was decided, however, that the air force share should be paid to the Royal Air Force charitable and welfare societies caring for present and past members of the service.
In Canada the government proposes not to take one-third off but to divide the whole

Canadian share in proportion to the numbers engaged on naval operations, which works out at sixty-eight per cent for the navy and thirty-two per cent for the air force.
In considering how the navy's share would be divided, the whole position was thoroughly reviewed. Obviously, on the British scales which are predicated	on	responsibility,officers, particularly	senior officers,	wouldbenefit substantially,	as	their	shares	wouldrun into considerable sums; but in the case of men, the share would be about $10 each if paid to all the sailors who had been on sea operations for six months or more. A distribution on this basis would, it was considered after careful examination, be very much less desired by naval personnel themselves than to have the money used by their own representatives	to	meet	needy	cases.
This was particularly desirable in view of the fact that the system of disposing of canteen profits in the navy resulted in the Royal Canadian Navy benevolent trust fund receiving less funds in proportion than those made available to the other services. Moreover, the fund is being expended at a rate which will speedily exhaust it. Accordingly, both the navy's share and the air force's share will be paid into the trust funds for the benefit of veterans and members of these services. In other words, a distribution to individual personnel would involve a gain of small consequence to those who might be eligible, but by the method proposed the scope of assistance to those who are in genuine distress will be materially greater.
It was felt that the great majority of veterans and active force personnel concerned would want the money to be used to help former comrades and their families who are in need.

speechtext:
The house resumed from Monday, February 7, consideration of the motion of Mr. Garson that the house go into committee to consider the following resolution:
That it is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I sincerely hope that the contents of this resolution for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council does not constitute the whole of the program the government intends to bring in at this session in connection with the very serious matter of prices and distribution facing the country today.
The people of Canada are expecting effective government action at this session relative to the present unprecedented high cost of living. The rank and file of the Canadian people are not asking for more controls; but they are asking for relief from the burden of high living costs. People generally are waking up to the fact that the government itself is perhaps the chief culprit in this whole matter of extremely high prices. I claim the government has contributed very largely to the making of any emergency which does exist at the present time, four years after the close of the war.
For example, the people of Canada are aware that the Liberal government last year overtaxed them by at least $600 million in hidden and indirect taxes alone, which taxes were added to the price the consumers had to pay for the things they have to buy from day to day. Perhaps the most vicious of all these hidden taxes is the sales tax.
I was much interested in the excellent speech delivered in the debate on the address in reply to the speech from the throne by the hon. member for Beauce (Mr. Dionne), an experienced manufacturer. In his speech he illustrated the bad effects of the government's eight per cent sales tax, and showed clearly that this tax, applied at the manufacturer's level to, for instance, $100 worth of cotton goods-I believe he mentioned shirting-often pyramids to $30, or 30 per cent of the manufacturer's price by the time the goods reach the consumer.
We need only look around us and do a little investigating to find that on most articles we have to buy from day to day government taxes constitute up to as high as 74 or 76 per cent of the consumer price. I need not 29087-431
Transitional Measures Act go into details, because I am sure all hon. members have run into examples of the same thing.
This raises what I consider is a serious point for consideration, a point about which I have complained in this house on a number of occasions and about which I intend to complain now. During the last half century governments have moved in to prevent the people from realizing the benefits that should have accrued to them from technological improvements in machines and processes and manufacturing. As everyone who has studied the situation knows, through the use of machines things can be made today faster, cheaper and better than ever before.
But I ask this question: Can we buy them more cheaply than ever before? Certainly not. In the last fifty years improvements in machines have greatly reduced the real cost of production, but the benefits from the use of those machines have not been passed on to the consumer. Goods that are totally produced by machine today cost five or six times what they did in the day when they were totally made by the hand of man. The major reason for this is the fact that as savings have been effected by the improvement in processing and machines, governments have stepped in and have imposed scores of different kinds of hidden taxes at different levels of manufacture and production. As a result we have today sales taxes, processing taxes, turnover taxes, excise taxes of a dozen different varieties, and customs duties. All these things pyramid the costs of things to consumers.
Is it any wonder that under the circumstances the cost of living to the Canadian people is high? The people of Canada have a just right to complain about this high-handed and I would say tyrannous way in which the government has arrogated to itself, not only all the savings that have been effected in the cost of production through the use of machines but many more times these savings as well.
I have stated on a number of occasions and I repeat today my firm belief that the government is the main culprit in the high cost of living situation. However, I should like to point out that they are not alone responsible. Many Canadian industries have proceeded to price themselves out of future markets. Many of them have taken advantage of scarcities to charge all that the traffic will bear. That practice is reprehensible and I think the industries that have been guilty of it will in time come to see that it is not to their advantage let alone to the advantage of the Canadian people so to do.

Transitional Measures Act
I should like to point out another factor in this high cost of living situation that is rarely if ever considered. The C.C.F.-C.C.L. hook-up must shoulder a considerable share of the blame for the condition under which many Canadians actually suffer because their incomes are inadequate to enable them to pay the high prices for the things they need. The C.C.L. unions have been badly led and badly advised in their blind and determined drive for high wages. They have constantly refused to face facts, particularly the fact that when wages and salaries rise, costs also rise. That is inevitable. It is not just the amount of money that they get with which labour should be concerned; they should be concerned about the purchasing power that is available to them.

I shall have to answer part of
that "yes" and part of it "no". To the latter part I would have to say, "Definitely no." I say that for various reasons. As I said, it is the total of the purchasing power available to labour that measures its prosperity or the lack of it, and not the monetary return they receive. I say that, had the C.C.L. unions- this is in answer to my good friend, the hon. member for Cariboo (Mr. Irvine)-been better advised and led, their first efforts would have been directed toward holding the price line by a means that would not have discouraged the incentive for all-out production; that would not have imposed an unbearable burden of taxes upon the people.
That could have been done by insisting that whatever increases were won to supplement salary or wage incomes should not be first passed through the channels of industry in the form of salary or wage increases that enter and inflate costs. They were encouraged by the C.C.F. to believe that they should strike for higher wages and that the government would be driven to reimpose over-all price controls without wage controls, thus making all wage increases a net gain to labour. What has been the result? Organized labour did go out after higher wages, but the government did not impose over-all price control. Indeed they claimed that they could not do so in peacetime without imposing wage ceilings at the same time. The result was that production costs went up in an alarming fashion and of course consumer prices spiraled to new heights.
Once more we have had in this country a demonstration of the cat going around and around in an effort to catch its own tail. I

notice that the C.C.F. has not been so urgent of late in their demands for control.

speechtext: Give us a chance.

I realize that and the hon. member will have a chance. We used to hear a great deal from the C.C.F. about the superior economy which has been established in socialist Britain. I had the privilege of visiting Britain last autumn and was able to see something of the socialist planned economy and the results of the over-all government controls which have been imposed in that country. I certainly came away from Britain much more impressed with the far-reaching results of bureaucratic control than I was with any good that has been accomplished through them. Let me point out a few examples. These are only a few and I do not mean to be unfair to Britain when I mention them.
When we first got to Britain we found that according to a government order there was a ceiling of five shillings on meals in restaurants. However, we found that after we had ordered our meal and had eaten it, such as it was, they imposed a cover charge, a surcharge, a supercharge and a house charge in addition to the fairly substantial tip that we were expected to give.

I went into a small place which possibly the ' hon. member for Selkirk (Mr. Bryce) might call a joint. I do not know, but I tried to eat in various places. I noticed when I went into small luncheon places that a snack of fish and chips, a dark flour roll, and a cup of

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I am only pointing out to you-

But the price which they had to pay for the substitute for the real thing, this phony sausage, was away out of proportion to the value of the contents. Taking it all in all, I should like to say that, according to my observation, British bureaucracy is experiencing real difficulty in the enforcement of the controls which they have.	*
I observed also that when the general run of the British people got through providing themselves with the bare necessities of what I thought was a rather lacklustre and monotonous living, they had nothing left to put away for a rainy day. In that respect they are hardly any different from the general run of the Canadian people except that we in this country are much more fortunate in the variety and the quality of the things we buy.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speechtext: Oh, yes, it can. Don't ever get away with that idea.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

I think there is no doubt that in Great Britain all-out efforts to produce have been discouraged by the bureaucratic controls employed by the socialist government. Regimentation has been the poison that has killed the spirit of every nation down through history. It has killed the spirit of every nation which has imposed regimentation and bureaucratic control. I am convinced that regimentation and bureaucratic control will destroy Great Britain if the people suffer them to remain a major part of their economic life for very long.
The point I wish to emphasize is that there is nothing in the socialist British system of a controlled economy that commends itself for introduction in Canada. On the other

Transitional Measures Act hand, no one can deny that some worthwhile things have been done towards ensuring social justice to a good many people of that country. Any honest person must make that admission.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That has nothing whatever to do with it. The improvements, which they have made in social security for many of their people, have been things which could have been done just as well in other ways without involving bureaucratic control and regimentation. For their particular emergency, and there is no question that they have been in a state of emergency, doubtless some controls have been necessary; but in England and Scotland I met many well-informed people who believe that the final objective of the socialist intellectuals, who are now in control of the policy of the Labour government, is the complete sovietization of the people.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Oh, oh.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: That is absolute rot, undiluted rot.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: I repeat that in my journey through England and Scotland I met a good many people who sincerely and earnestly said they believe that the policy being advocated by the intellectual socialists who are in control of the policy of the Labour government is the final sovietization of the people of Great Britain.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Spoken like a fascist.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

Fortunately, Mr. Speaker, what I have just stated does not seem to be the desire of the bona fide trade unionists who have come up through the ranks of apprentice and journeyman, and into the master class. I spoke to a good many of them, and it appears to me that there is a growing and serious divergence of views between the two divisions of government supporters, the intellectual socialist who thinks he has an itch to control everybody's business, and the true trade unionist who is an honourable fellow who came up through the ranks in an honourable way.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS

speechtext:
-to this subject, just as one of their brain-trusters has done. I refer to Professor Frank W. Underhill, the distinguished Canadian socialist philosopher and co-author of the book "Social Planning for Canada", which our friends have been putting before the public for some years.
In an article written for the Canadian Forum of August, 1947, Professor Underhill had this to say:
-and when socialists keep on harping about controls as the essence of their policy, they lend plausibility to the charges that they are really frustrated bureaucrats with an itch to manage other people's business for them.
At another point in the same article, he says:
Still, the socialists should ease up on their persistent talk about controls. What the world needs chiefly at present is enterprise and imagination, initiative and vision. The defenders of capitalism are quite right in maintaining that these qualities were given full scope in the capitalism of the past and that this was the reason for the great material progress of recent generations. We still need enterprise.
Those are the words of the brain-truster of the socialist party of this country.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext: Head the next paragraph.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
It is evident that he has done a good deal of thinking since the time he wrote the book "Social Planning for Canada" or helped with the writing of it.
Today, the government is asking for an extension of certain control orders and regulations that were imposed by order in council during a real war emergency. It is not possible, sir, to get a full picture of the government's request from consideration of this one resolution, No. 5 on the order paper. To get a complete picture it is necessary to consider, along with resolution No. 5, the resolution on foreign exchange; the resolution on the Agricultural Products Act; the resolution on the export and import of fish and fish containers; and resolution No. 6 in connection with the Canadian Commercial Corporation Act.
If the powers requested in these resolutions are granted, the government will then have control over foreign exchange, agricultural products, rentals and price ceilings on flour, bread, butter, citrus fruits, imported canned citrus fruit juices, certain imported fresh vegetables, onions, certain fresh fruits,

molasses and sugar. In addition to that, there will be steel control, timber control and price control of certain steel products. This represents a sizeable centralization of power under present-day conditions.
When these various resolutions are before the house, I take it the minister concerned will make a statement to justify the request contained in those resolutions. There should be justification, particularly, of the continuation of control by the procedure which is being followed, namely, by resolution and continuing orders in council, rather than by specific acts of this parliament.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I say that the people of this country are going to be bitterly disappointed if the government fails to supplement these orders, which are now in the form of resolutions, by positive action aimed at reducing the cost of living. I declare there is no better place to start than in their own taxation structure, especially the iniquitous sales tax. This tax is not an economic necessity. It is an instrument of policy which pushes up the cost of living by fully 20 per cent. At the polls, sir, the people of Canada are going to show their extreme displeasure if this tax and a number of other nuisance taxes are not abolished. If at this session this government does not make a substantial effort to bring down the cost of living to a reasonable level by eliminating the sales tax and using the modest subsidies which we have proposed from time to time on selected items used from day to day by families, which subsidies could be paid for not out of taxation but with interest-free money, then the people of the country will be disappointed. With a single stroke the government can cure the major cause of the high cost of living. The people of this country are demanding action along the lines I have suggested, Mr. Speaker.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
The resolution before the house this afternoon, Mr. Speaker, reads as follows:
Resolved, that It is expedient to introduce a measure to provide for the continuation of certain orders and regulations of the governor in council for a limited period during the national emergency arising out of the war.
In 1947 we had before us the first one of these orders for continuing the emergency powers that had been granted the government during the war. At that particular time, I believe there were some fifty-seven of them and the Minister of Justice of the day told us each one of these controls contained a principle. It is the principle contained in these control measures of which I wish to speak this afternoon.
A similar debate dealing with the continuation of controls was held in 1948. Last week,
Transitional Measures Act on the 7th of February, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) gave us some indication of the controls it was proposed to continue. We have not been told whether it is proposed to continue them for one year or two years. At that time, in dealing with one of the controls, steel control, the Minister of Trade and Commerce said, as reported at page 317 of Hansard:
We have been importing roughly 30 per cent of all the steel that is used, and those imports have been obtained with a great deal of difficulty.
For a few moments, Mr. Speaker, I propose to deal with the matter of steel control. I am quite prepared to admit that what the minister says is true. We have been importing 30 per cent of our steel and he has had a great deal of trouble in obtaining it. As I see it, however, that is his job as Minister of Trade and Commerce, and probably he has done a very good job. In respect of this measure of steel control, we have also the continuing powers of the steel controller, which is quite a different thing, so far as I am concerned. It is about the continuation of those powers that I wish to speak.
Through the press, the steel controller has reported what he considers our position to be in respect to steel in 1949. In the Globe and Mail on the 27th of January last, he said:
Makers of all steel products from cans to cars and bolts to bridges can look for steel supplies to be no better and no worse in 1949 than they were in 1948.
Then he goes on to say:
Canadian production this year should be up by about 75,000 product tons from last year's 2,300,000, but the import from United States will be down by about 120,000. The difference which makes the outlook "about the same for 1949," will be made up by increased supplies from Belgium, Austria, the United Kingdom, and other European sources.
I suppose we have to depend upon the steel controller for information concerning our position in 1949 and what provision we are going to make for industry to proceed as it should. I suppose he ought to know the situation at first hand. But on the other hand his report is not the only one that appears in the papers. The Canadian Manufacturers Association's special committee on steel met within the last month. They issued a statement to the effect that, as to United States mills, there are positive signs that the pressure for delivery of steel is easing up, and that the prospect is that by the third quarter of 1949 a buyers' market will develop in some steel products. It is this matter of steel that the government is seeking to control in this bill. The quotation continues:
While there has been no apparent move on the part of the United States or Canadian governments to enlarge the nominal Canadian import quota of

Transitional Measures Act 200,000 to 220,000 product tons of steel per quarter, the only actual control exercised over imported steel in Canada has been the rather loose one on structural steel.
That is a report from people who are in the business. It is a report from a committee of steel manufacturers. They tell us that by the third quarter of 1949 steel will be easier. In fact, they go on to say that there is quite a chance that the production and use of steel may be almost on an even footing. Just yesterday another report came from New York through the Associated Press. I should like to quote from it:
Steel people believe that the next sixty days "will answer a lot of questions" as to extent of demand for steel, the "Iron Age" metalworking trade weekly said.
Noting that some American companies are planning capacity operations into June, the publication said: "They don't say June will be the turning point, they simply are unwilling to guess too far ahead."
Going to the second last paragraph of the article, I find it reads as follows:
For the fifth consecutive week, steel production in the United States has been maintained at an annual rate of more than 97 million tons. The first quarter of this year, the publication said, probably will see an all-time record for production of steel.
It continues: "Every week the industry continues this tremendous production pace it moves the market factors of supply and demand nearer to the point of balance. Some people inside and outside the steel industry are beginning to wonder what will happen when that precarious point is reached- possibly during this year."
So I am pointing out to the minister and through him to the steel controller that, as a matter of fact, there are in the industry people who seem to think that during this year we shall reach a point where we shall have not only in the United States but here in Canada sufficient steel for our purposes.
How is this control exercised here in Canada? Last year the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) told us, when he was dealing with the matter of the import and export bill, that there was no restriction on steel coming through from the United States, that we would take all the steel we could get. I understand, and the minister will correct me if 1 am wrong, that the practice is for the manufacturing concerns in the United States to ship their steel directly across to those of our Canadian buyers who wish to buy steel from them, and that in that respect there is little or no control; we take all the steel that we can get, with this one exception of structural steel. I believe the Department of Trade and Commerce, under the export and import act, exercises some control over the fabricator of steel and says that this steel may go to such and such a project and that other steel shall go to such and such another project.
Last year when I was speaking on this matter I asked the minister if there would
TMr. Timmins.]
be steel for theatres, and I believe his answer was that there would not be. I also asked him if there would be steel for office buildings, and I remember pointing out one particular office building that was going up. The answer by the minister was that steel would not be allowed for that project. As I pass the building from day to day, however, and see it progressing, I see that it has steel and that it is an office building. If we are to have control in respect of steel in our own country, there should be some formula or some plan so that we might know who may have steel, in what quantities, and for what purposes.
The emergency control order which we saw last year, and which I presume may be presented again in somewhat the same fashion this year, is a fairly all-embracing one, giving wide powers. As it is said

and I believe it to be true-that we are getting to the point where steel in Canada before this year is out will be in sufficient quantity that we can do what our manufacturers and our people want to do, it seems to me that there should be some relief from these controls instead of a further measure of increase of them. Before the debate is over I should like the Minister of Trade and Commerce to reaffirm what he said last year about what was needed and what kind of permit would be given with respect to the delivery of structural steel.
Within the industry itself there are some controls exercised by either the steel controller or the Department of Trade and Commerce-and I was under the impression that it was through the Department of Trade and Commerce-whereby, as the minister said as reported at page 317 of Hansard:
We are also moving semi-finished steel from the Dominion Steel and Coal Company at Sydney to Hamilton, to the extent of about 10,000 tons per month. That 28,000 tons of steel, which cannot be finished at Algoma or at Sydney, would ordinarily go for export and be finished in other countries. That was the pre-war history of the surpluses of those two plants. By moving that steel to Hamilton 28,000 tons per month of additional basic steel are turned into finished products.
I think that is all to the good. It helps us to keep up employment in our own country and it helps the industries to work between each other and complement their various plants; and I suppose to some extent the price at which the finishing is done is fixed through the control order. But the fact of the matter is that under these controls the situation is getting to the point where a plant may survive or perish depending on how the controls are exercised. I was in a plant in which they were doing what I presume would be called metal stamping. I found that they were working only at about 50 per cent capacity because, as they said, they could not

get sufficient steel to carry on with, and it was all subject to what they could get from Canadian firms through the controller of steel. They also told me that they had not been able to take an order in almost a year because they did not know what the future was to be in respect of production.

The point I wanted to make was this. When I asked for permission to use the material and to give the names of the manufacturers who were involved in this matter, I found that there was a great deal of resistance on their part to being quoted in any way. This is no reflection on the minister, but the fact of the matter is that the industry is so much in the hands of the Department of Trade and Commerce and of the steel controller that they just could not afford to be complaining openly for fear that their steel might be curtailed to a point where they could not carry on. When we get the steel industry of the country in that position, then we are getting to the point where there is dictation. I am not suggesting to the minister that he is dictating, but I do say that we are in a trend, and the control trend is increasing to such a point that if we do not watch ourselves this whole industry will be under control. If one refers back to the control measure of last year, and examines the controls that are contained in that measure, he will easily discover that there is hardly anything the controller of steel cannot do. He can even go out and prospect for iron ore. He can run a smelting mill; he can run a melting mill; he can take possession of steel wherever he finds it. He can sell it for whatever price he wishes; he can run a refinery, a foundry and a warehouse. He can fix and regulate prices. There is hardly anything that he cannot do. He can do all this at a time when indications would seem to show that we are coming out of a shortage of steel.
I was disturbed when I read what the controller of steel had to say the other day as reported in the press. He said:
I do not wish to detract from the magnificent increases in production which have been achieved by the Canadian steel industry since 1939, but merely to point out that if Canada is now fully developed from the viewpoint of steel production, the United States and Great Britain are hopelessly overdeveloped.
Transitional Measures Act
He went on to say:
The United States does not take the latter view. The United States is prepared to give assistance to expansion, and "if the industry is not prepared to expand with governmental assistance, the expansion will be effected by the government without recourse to the industry."
I do not believe that these words were used with respect to Canada. I believe they were used with respect to the United States, but a little later on referring to Canada he said:
As for government assistance, he thought it unlikely the government "would go into the steel business by creating any plants of its own but would make loans for the expansion plans of others."
Then he went on to say:
Every ton of steel made in Canada has a definite home at least sixty days before it rolls off the production line. For this reason, if the flow of steel to a particular project must be increased, it can be done only at the expense of other users.
"It is for that reason," he said, "that those enterprises which are being supported by the government have been confined to a small number of projects of a national character."
This quotation from the controller of steel would seem to indicate that there is a trend to increase the control of steel. Perhaps some of the powers that we had in the bill last year and which are to be brought forward this year will lead us into new fields in which the government will be taking an active part. So far as I am concerned, this is a matter which, just as quickly as the government can do it, should be left to the people who are in the enterprise. If we are ever to get this country on its feet the one hope that we have of obtaining enough United States dollars is in the production of iron ore and the fabrication of steel in this country. The day will probably come, and I hope it will come soon, when this industry will be the saviour of the economy of Canada. I hope that by its own efforts it will bring itself to the point where we shall produce sufficient iron and steel so that we shall have enough United States dollars to carry on with. When we come to the bill itself I hope we shall see that a great many of these powers that were contained in the bill of 1948 will not be carried forward in the 1949 bill. I hope that a great number of these powers which the controller of steel has been using up to this time, or could fall back on, may be discarded.
I understand that we are to have a new controller before very long. Perhaps this will be the time at which we should make these reductions in control because we do not want the new controller to begin his duties with the same thoughts in mind as the present controller seems to have, namely, that the government might get into the steel business.
I should like now to say a word or two about rental control. I presume we shall have the

Transitional Measures Act same bill before us this year as we had last year. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) has already said what his proposals in the matter were going to be. At page 316 of Hansard he said:
As the house is aware the government announced some time ago that it proposed to ask parliament to authorize the continuance ot rental controls until March 31, 1950, and that provision would be made in the order continuing that control to provide that the dominion government would withdraw from that field in any province where the province requested that it do so, and that parliament would also be asked to make provision for paying the costs for one year of rental controls in any province which might see fit to exercise control in that particular field.
The minister knows full well that rental control, whether by good judgment or bad, was brought about by this government in 1945. He knows that the solution does not lie in throwing the responsibility onto someone else when all the mechanism of dealing with the housing situation, which is at the bottom of it all, rests with the federal government itself. As a matter of fact, how could the provinces hope to do anything in the realm of housing, which is our major problem today, when timber control is entirely in the hands of the federal government? In addition to that, steel control is in the hands of the federal government, and out of steel control emanates the production or non-production of bathtubs, basins, hardware, soil pipe, furnaces, and so on. All these things are under the control of the federal government. Further than that, building priorities are a subject matter that the federal government has stuck close to and still holds on to in order to produce the type of house that they think should be produced in Canada. So long as these elements are in the hands of the federal government it is useless for the minister to say that we shall turn this over to some other government who will do the job from that point on. As a matter of fact, the federal government has no housing program for Canada. It simply stumbles on, from year to year, telling us two or three times each year how many houses have been produced in that year, mostly by private enterprise, and then telling us that next year so many more houses will be produced. If the government would take this problem by the throat, shake it a bit, and then shake themselves, we would probably have some houses built in Canada. When we had the houses we might consider doing something about this rent control measure. Until such time however as the government really gets hot about this matter of producing houses, the matter of rent control will stand where it is.
It would not be so bad if we did not see so many anomalies under rent control. For instance, I believe the people of Canada, by

reason of rent control regulations, in a sense are losing faith in themselves in the matter of looking after their own housing rights and responsibilities. For instance, how many tens of thousands of Canadian people have had to look to someone else to provide them with the kind of accommodation they have been unable to produce themselves. And there are thousands of others still living in accommodation not fit for human habitation.
Further when the government seeks to put through amendments to rental orders, I say it is in duty bound to see that it makes workable amendments, instead of the sloppy and inefficient amendments which do harm to hundreds, perhaps thousands, of good Canadian citizens. For instance in November of 1948 an amendment was made to the rental order which provided that an owner who had been owner of a property on November 1, 1947, could give six months' notice to the tenant to vacate, provided the landlord needed the accommodation for himself.
That was a sloppy amendment. It has struck more fear and terror to and caused more anguish in the hearts of more people throughout this country than any other provision in any amendment to a control measure. As a matter of fact, when the tenant receives such six months' notice he does not have a chance in those six months to find out whether the landlord actually needs the property, and is going to be able to prove his need before a judge or not. The result is, there is no way for the tenant to know whether he is going to be put out at the end of six months, or whether the notice is invalid and he should pay no attention to it.
The fact of the matter is that, after two or three months, not being able to get any satisfaction, and not knowing what his position is, he tries to find ways and means of getting other accommodation, often of an inferior type, when, as a matter of fact, if at the beginning he had been given an opportunity upon receipt of the notice to go before a judge and have the matter decided, he could have known whether, at the end of six months, he would have to move or not.
In addition to that, the amendment does not show in what legal jurisdiction the decision is to be made. There is no commissioner, such as applies in respect to other regulations under the rental orders. The decision would probably be made by a county court judge; but the county court judge does not get his authority from the rental order, but rather from the landlord and tenancy act of the province in which the tenant may be living.
So that, in respect of probably a thousand notices now being given, there are a thousand

families in Toronto who do not know today whether or not they can be put out six months hence. Those of us in the House of Commons have some responsibilities in respect to what amendments are made by the minister's department. To be a party to the sort of amendment I have described does not reflect any credit upon the minister or upon us.
By reason of the various amendments made to the rental order, without any thought to the housing situation, in Toronto today there are about four thousand people who on the first of May or June next will be evicted, if judges make orders against them, and who will be forced to try to find some other accommodation. This happens at a time when the government takes no responsibility whatsoever in respect to a real housing program.
Last year those of us who spoke on rental control suggested that, if this control was to be continued, some further relief should be given to veterans. Perhaps it was intended that the amendment of 1948, of which I have just spoken, would give that relief. I do believe however that at this time the minister ought to give thought to bringing that relief to the veteran who, prior to December 31, 1948, had acquired a home and paid for it, and who finds it necessary to get into that home. It seems to me that in all circumstances a veteran, on six months' notice, ought to have the opportunity to get into his own home, if he purchased it prior to December 31, 1948. I suggest the minister should give some thought to this matter.
Finally, speaking generally in respect to control of prices, we know that just this week the court of appeal sitting in Toronto handed down a decision in the McGinn case. That was a case in which a hardware merchant had been convicted of selling nails in contravention of section 8 of the wartime prices and trade board order at a price that was higher than was reasonable and just. In that particular instance, the man dealing in the nails -I believe he was a builder who dealt in nails rather than, in the strict sense, a hardware merchant-made a profit of $3,661.48 on 1,532 kegs of nails, when the average profit would have been $965.16.
I do not believe the court of appeal handed down a written judgment. My information is that the judgment was delivered orally. It may be that someone took down in shorthand the effect of the judgment but, as I say, I understand it was delivered orally. Perhaps reasons for judgment will now be forthcoming. The fact of the matter seems to be, however, that the court of appeal felt that the expression "higher than is reasonable or just" is so general in its application, 29087-44J
Transitional Measures Act and lacked such definition, that it could not possibly permit the conviction to stand.
Last year the government told us that in respect of control of rising prices two remedies could be had. The first was that under the Combines Investigation Act a person who did not play the game in the matter of prices could be brought to book or that, under the wartime prices and trade board order, there was provision to look after the man who was a shyster and who took advantage of the situation to make exorbitant profits. Now we seem to be down to only the Combines Investigation Act. In that connection I was interested to read again the conclusions of the committee on prices which sat last year, to see if, having regard to the decision in the McGinn case, the Canadian public could take any comfort out of the committee's conclusion with regard to prices.
Conclusion 11 of the committee reads:
The committee realizes that in the long run the federal government may be faced with constitutional difficulties in regard to its operations in the field of prices. This is clearly a matter in which, within the Canadian federal structure, responsibility normally rests with the provincial governments, although the federal government, under wartime emergency conditions, was compelled to take action in this field.
The committee is therefore forced to the conclusion that the solution of the problem of the adequate protection of the Canadian consumer will require the co-operation of the provincial governments with the federal government by taking the measures required in meeting their responsibilities.
That just lands us simply nowhere. I suggest to the minister in connection with the McGinn case, either that it be appealed right away, or that he see to it that the wartime prices and trade board order be given some teeth with respect to prices.

maintopic: TRANSITIONAL MEASURES ACT, 1947 CONTINUATION OF CERTAIN ORDERS AND REGULATIONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in my opinion this measure with regard to our domestic policy is the most important measure we have had before us this session. Under the authority of this resolution it is proposed to introduce a bill which will continue certain orders and regulations that were exercised during the war. Of course the principal part will be that dealing with prices and the authority under which price control has been exercised.
I am glad the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott) is in his seat. Although the resolution is in the name of the Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson), in this case he is only the innocent bystander-he is only giving the bride away. The main proposal has been made by the Minister of Finance and it is chiefly to him I wish to refer when I refer to the government.
About a year ago this house set up a special committee to investigate the price situation in this country. There were those

Transitional Measures Act in this group who said that it would be a waste of money and time to set up a committee which would only make excuses for the policies of the government. That committee, together with the royal commission which is still operating and which is about to make its report, will cost this country about $100,000.
One of the duties of parliament at this time is to assess the work done by the special committee-we have not the means available to assess the work of the commission as yet- to look at its proposals or recommendations and decide whether the government is doing or has done anything to carry out the recommendations of the committee or to warrant the time and money expended in gathering that information.
I contend that the government has made no attempt whatsoever to carry out the rec-ommendatijns of the prices committee which worked so hard under difficult conditions. The Minister of Finance is the chief culprit in making a complete farce of the work of that committee. I was astounded when this matter first came before the house to see the Minister of Finance blithely get up in his place and give us a preview of the bill which is to follow this resolution. That was a most unusual course to follow because on other occasions when we were anxious to find out something about bills that were to come at a future time we were told, "Oh, no, we cannot tell you anything about the bill until the resolution is passed." On this occasion, with only the slightest encouragement, the minister was apparently glad to give us a running account of what is to be contained in the bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: It was just my naturally frank nature.

Perhaps. Although I am not of a particularly suspicious nature I wonder if it was not a bit of appeasement; I wonder if the minister was not trying to forestall the hue and cry that is bound to be raised in this house and elsewhere over the government control of prices and its carrying on in a bureaucratic manner. I think the minister was just a little too anxious to get out from under. He was just a little bit anxious to say to the powers that be, "Do not worry yourselves too much; this bill is going to be even less insignificant than the bill of a year ago." He said that it was going to cover a restricted field and a rapidly diminishing one. In other words, this is going to be a decontrol bill.
After having read the report of the special committee and the publicity in connection with the royal commission, many people were under the misapprehension that something would be done. The royal commission carried on a tremendous task in gathering mate-


rial and hearing witnesses and no doubt will be making recommendations. But before the report of that commission is even tabled in this house, the government is telling it that its work has been wasted, that it has made up its mind not to impose controls but to propose a decontrol bill which would cover a restricted field and a rapidly diminishing one.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Does my hon. friend suggest that the commission was set up to recommend controls?
If the commission was not set up to make recommendations, I wonder why it was set up at all?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I am asking the hon. member if he thinks it was set up to suggest controls?

I did not say that. I said
that even before the tabling of the commission's report the government is telling the house and the commission what it proposes to do; it is telling them that it is going to present a decontrol bill.
Before referring to the actual report of the special committee on prices, I should like to consider for a time the situation in the country, which is creating concern in the minds of the people of Canada. I have never argued in this house or elsewhere that high prices as such were a burden upon the people, or that inflation in itself was the chief evil in this country. High prices or inflation are burdensome only to the extent that they create injustice in the distribution of prices across the country.
If there is a general rise in prices affecting all producers and all other people equally, then the only harm that is done is the inconvenience of having to carry a bigger pocket-book. But when the prices of the products of some people are going down while the prices of the things they have to buy are going up, a real injustice is created. That is where price control comes in.
By that proposition it follows that price control is not, as some people seem to think, merely a matter of keeping prices down. It is a matter of keeping prices properly adjusted so that no injustice shall be done to any occupational group in the country. That is the responsibility of the government, whether they admit it or not. There is one occupational group in this country, the primary producing group which would include farmers, fishermen and ranchers, that is seriously concerned at this time because it is beginning to see a trend similar to what happened approximately twenty years ago.
If any one had said in 1929 that it was necessary to have price control many people

would have laughed, would have said, "What for?" At that time prices were quite reasonable. The primary producers were receiving a fair return for their products in relation to the prices of the manufactured products they had to buy. But in a brief space of time what happened? I have the figures here to show the double-barreled trend that came upon us so suddenly that the people were completely unprepared. At that time we had what is now known as a depression. Some people blamed that on spots on the sun while others claimed it was due to certain mystic causes.
It was in socialist countries as well.

Would you name those
socialist countries?
New Zealand and Australia.
My friend had better study his history as well as his law books because in 1929, 1930 and 1931 they did not have socialist governments.
But after they came into power the people still suffered.

The Labour government of
New Zealand did not come into power until 1935. Now that we have our history straightened out let us go on. There was a double-barreled trend that hit the country all at once, and particularly the primary producers, with the prices of farm products taking a sudden drop and the prices of manufactured products leisurely taking their time about coming down, and in some cases not coming down at all but going up. The Minister of Justice (Mr. Garson) will remember the time when the price of wheat was dropping by ten or twelve cents a day, and at the same time the prices of farm implements were actually increasing. I have figures here which illustrate the situation as to prices for cattle and hogs. The table is as follows:
Cattle and. Hog Prices, December, 1933
Per 100 lbs.
Hogs	 $5.43
Beef Steers	 3.00
Cows	 1.45
Bulls	 1.38
You could feed a multitude of people with the price of a cow at $1.45 per hundred pounds. In 1934 the Robert Simpson Company was doing fairly well. I have figures showing that on certain types of clothing they made profits ranging from 101 per cent to 374 per cent at the same time that farmers were giving away their produce for practically nothing. In some cases the cost of trans-
Transitional Measures Act portation was more than the value of the animal shipped.
Was that gross or net profit?
That is the percentage of profit in relation to cost.
Gross profit.
What are you quoting from?

I am glad that question was asked. The figures are taken from the report of the special committee on price spreads and mass buying. The chairman of that committee was Hon. H. H. Stevens, who was appointed by the Bennett administration.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: It is markup, is it not?

That is the percentage of profit in relation to cost. It is the markup, and that would be the gross profit. When we are talking about gross profit and net profit it might be just as well to quote the figures of total farm income for comparable years. I cited the year 1934 in relation to the profits of the Robert Simpson Company. According to the Dominion Bureau of Statistics the gross income per farm in Canada was $535, and the net income was, if you please, $98 per farm.
If you take the total income it makes it even worse. I think it was only $86 million.
That makes it worse.

The reason I am putting these figures before the house is to show that price control is not merely nor chiefly a matter of holding prices down. It is a matter of adjusting prices in order to make them fair to all concerned. As I mentioned on a previous occasion not so long ago, the main objective of the primary producers of the country, as expressed through their organization, the Canadian federation of agriculture, is the stabilization of their position. Farmers today are prepared to carry their share of the load, but they do not wish to see their prices diminishing while other prices are still climbing, and thus be given an unfair share in carrying the burden of the country's economy. I think that is a reasonable position to take. It should be one of the chief objectives of the house to work out a program under which agriculture will be stabilized in the future, and without a measure of price control I do not know how it can be done.
I want to say with all sincerity that when I read the various party platforms I find much in their proposals for agriculture with which I can agree; but frankly I fail to see how any of them can be carried out unless we

Transitional Measures Act have a system of price control in order to stabilize the economy of our country. All parties start out by saying something like this: "We believe in giving the farmers a fair share of the national income." How are you going to do that under a system of free enterprise if the trend is the same as it was in the period of ten years from 1929 to 1939? Under free enterprise what government of that day could have given the farmers a fair share of the national income, and what government made any attempt to do so? Therefore, if we are going to carry out the pledges to the Canadian people that we have made in our election platforms, we must carry them through to the point where we are willing to accept responsibility in the house for providing and setting up machinery which will do what the various party platforms say they will do for agriculture.
To return to the report of the special committee on price spreads and mass buying, the chief question that arises is, who is responsible for the increase in prices. I am not going to say that all the responsibility lies in one quarter, but I do say that the chief villain in the drama is the profits that have been taken by various industries. There are those who will challenge that statement; there are others who will say that profits are not the main cause of price increases. Let me refer them to a newspaper clipping I have of a public opinion poll taken in July, 1947. The heading is: "Big profits are pointed to as the number one price villian." On reading it I was interested to find that they not only gave figures about public opinion on the question as a whole, but they also broke it down by political parties. I am not saying it is perfectly accurate, but it gives us a general picture. The question was asked: "Do you think the main cause of high prices in Canada is high wages, big profits or some other cause?" Fifty-five per cent answered, "big profits". More than half of the people of Canada said that big profits were the cause of high prices. When we come down to the party groupings we find that 54 per cent of the Liberals questioned admitted that the main cause was high profits. Forty-five per cent of the Conservatives questioned said the main cause was high profits, while only 35 per cent of the Conservatives said that it was high wages. Then it goes on to show that 72 per cent of the C.C.F. said that the main cause was high profits. That gives us an indication at least of the general public opinion on the question in 1947. I believe that nothing that has happened since that time has had any effect in changing their opinion. If anything, their opinion would be reinforced, because on the whole profits in 1948 were higher than they were in 1947.
[Mr. ZaplitnyJ

What did the committee on price spreads and mass buying say? First of all I will quote from page 4 of the report which is in the section dealing with their findings. I read:
In its investigations the committee found that, in certain instances, opportunists, taking advantage of the special conditions existing, made unprecedented profits. While it may be true in some cases that such profits were of a non-recurring type, there is no doubt that the high prices that produced these profits did raise the cost of living at that time.
That is a very mild way of putting it, but it is admitted that the profits involved were the cause in that instance of prices going up.
Then, on page 8, under recommendations, the committee says:
The government should give consideration to the desirability and practicability of restricting price rises by special taxation of unreasonable profits.
If they were not unreasonable profits, why would the committee recommend a special tax on them. It is a clear indication that the committee felt very uneasy about the unreasonable profits that were being taken.
On the tenth page of that report, the' committee makes a direct recommendation asking the government to consider the reimposition of certain control measures and the application of some measure of temporary subsidy. The committee which sat during last session made that direct recommendation. This committee cost the country $88,000, and the government has already announced, through the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), that it is tossing the report aside and is not going to act upon it.
We go further through the report and on page 24 we find these words:
-there can be no doubt from the experience of the committee that unreasonable and unjust profits and prices have been brought to light.
On page 25, we find these words:
-there were indications also that it represented in some exceptional cases a selfish attitude of trying to get the most out of the public without regard to the well-being of the consumer. This contention is based on the theory that so long as the public will pay a higher price, a higher price may be charged.
This is a reference to the attitude taken by various companies on the question of what constituted a fair price. The president of Canada Packers in his classic reply said that the price policy of the company was to buy as cheaply as possible and sell as high as possible.
What are you doing?

That seems to be the attitude all the way through. Some members ask me, "Is there anyone who has not that attitude?" A little while ago we heard from the member for Peace River (Mr. Low), who told us it was a most reprehensible thing for anyone to take advantage of the condition in the country by

extracting as much as possible in the way of profits. If that is a proper thing to do, as some members seem to think, if that is the proper way to carry on under a private enterprise system, then we might as well say so and throw it wide open.
Will the hon. member permit a question? Is that not the way he operates his own farm or his own business?

I am not going to argue about my private business. As it happens, I do not buy or sell things. The main point, however, is whether we are going to accept the proposition that it is proper for any industry or business in this country to gouge the customer as much as possible. If we accept that principle, there is no further argument. There is no need for this bill at all. On the other hand, if we accept the principle that our first concern should be for the public, that human rights take priority over property rights, then it is necessary for this house to provide legislation which will keep prices at a proper level. We can take one stand or the other.
When in doubt one likes to seek expert advice. This time, I am going to call a witness who, I think, will be acceptable to all members of the house in spite of some of the unkind things that have been said about him in the past. I still believe he was a faithful and loyal citizen doing a fine job in a difficult position. I refer to the former chairman of the wartime prices and trade board, Mr. Donald Gordon. During 1946, he made several broadcasts in which he frankly put before the Canadian people the choice they must make and the things that must be kept in mind in making that choice with relation to price control generally. I should like to quote a remark he made on the 1st of November, 1946.
People that want price increases sometimes suggest that removing the controls at this time would not result in any serious advance in the price level. That is sheer nonsense. That sort of view is the kind of logic used by an ostrich when he hides his head in the sand.
I am not going to make any comment on that remark, but I shall go to the next quotation, which is from a speech made on the 15th of November, 1946.
So, we Canadians haVe to make our choice-to decide whether the readjustments needed in present abnormal conditions should be controlled or uncontrolled. If our choice is to let the readjustment take place without government supervision or control, then we must be prepared to accept sudden and sharp advances in prices of many necessities and a condition of near-chaos in the field of shelter.
Those words were borne out by the argument of the hon. member who spoke just before me. I continue with the quotation:
We must also be prepared to take the very serious risk-in my view, it is a certainty-of a following
Transitional Measures Act slump in prices, in employment, in incomes and especially in farm incomes. Every lesson of the past shows how booms are followed by slumps. It seems to me that this fact must be one of the main certainties we must all have before us because assumptions to the contrary have been so consistently disproven.
In those few lines he not only pointed out, as far back as 1946, that if price controls were removed we would have to expect immediately the higher prices and hardships which we have been experiencing in the past few years; he also warned that, when the peak had been reached and passed, we must expect a sudden slump in prices in this country. We in western Canada who have seen the years of depression and the effect they had on the farm population know very well what he means by a sudden slump in farm income. Any member coming from the prairies or any member coming from a farming community should take that warning seriously, because as surely as we allow profiteering to run hog-wild, as surely as we allow industry to form combines and create monopolies in order to create artificial prices, then just as surely are we going to have another depression in this country. All the horrors, suffering and privation will be experienced again.
I could quote many more of Mr. Gordon's statements but I think I have quoted enough to indicate that, in his opinion, we could either throw the doors wide open and leave our price structure to speculation and profiteering, which seems to be the course some members in this house wish to take, including the Minister of Finance (Mr. Abbott), or we could have what has been described as a planned economy. The planned economy was scoffed at by the hon. member for Peace River (Mr. Low), but such scoffing was in poor taste because, in order to implement the social credit theory, it would require the most meticulously planned economy. In any event, we believe there must be planning on a national scale in order to see that the interests of the public are protected. I am sure the members of this house who are fond of reading should read a book entitled "Sweden, the Middle Way". It was written quite a few years ago and if it were rewritten to bring it up to date, it would be even more interesting. It is, however, one of the best books I have read to show what a democratic people can do in planning their economy, step by step, through co-operatives and so on. There is some private enterprise in that country as well. Sweden has natural resources similar to those in Canada, but not as much wealth; yet Sweden has managed to obtain a standard of living equal to any and to keep prices at a reasonable level at a time when
688	HOUSE OF
Transitional Measures Act other countries have been experiencing either , booms or slumps.
It seems to me, if this house is going to make a decision, it will have to be based on a knowledge of prices. There are those who throw up their hands in horror if you mention control to them in any shape or form. They scream for free enterprise. No one is opposed to free enterprise in its legitimate form. May I remind the members that as far back as 1934 or 1935, at a time when we were in a slight depression, we had just gone through a period in which we had the closest thing to free enterprise we ever had in this country.
All during the years of the depression we had no wheat board. There was no wartime prices and trade board, no rent control or control of any kind. Yet at the end of that period, as was well borne out by the report of the Stevens prices commission, it was found necessary to recommend to this parliament that certain forms of control be provided for in this house. Unfortunately, before many of those recommendations could be carried out, parliament was dissolved, there was an election in which the administration was defeated and a new government came in which of course tossed the whole thing out.

I deplore this attack upon Great Britain. The state in which she found herself was that of bankruptcy-a bankruptcy which was caused by her war effort. Everyone knows that. And, if I may say so, that war effort was not exerted wholly on her own behalf. Let us not forget that for many days and months she stood alone. Let us not forget that after the war her foreign trade had gone, her foreign investments had gone, but that she did her share-and did it nobly-of feeding the starving people of Europe.
What did she do? There would have been some excuse for her if she had thrown up her hands, as many other countries would have done. But no, not the Britisher; he sat down and made plans. So far as I am concerned, this procedure of sneering at planning does not apply to Great Britain, because she planned, and planned to some purpose. She went to work and made the best arrangement she could with her creditors. And let me say that she did not try to meet her debts with funny money, either.
She clamped down on her people for the purpose of carrying out a severe program through which her export trade might be gained back again. The hon. member sneered at the food over there. And, incidentally, they are free men.

The food does lack variety; of course it does. It is plain, but there is ample supply, and it is well distributed. Statistics of the social welfare department in England show that on the average children are both taller and heavier than they were a few years ago.

I will say this howqver that, in all the trips I have made over there, this was the first time I did not find the farmers complaining. And when you find farmers who do not complain you can conclude that they are fairly well satisfied.
For the first time farm labour is contented in spite of the assertions that come from many quarters that that cannot be brought about. They have proved that it can be done, that farm labour can be placed on a basis of decent wages and decent working hours.
The district to which I refer happens to be in the north of Ireland. It is interesting to note that the government there is perhaps the only Tory government in the world, certainly in the commonwealth, with the exception of the one my hon. friends over here are interested in, in the province of Ontario. It is called a Tory government but it does not qualify as such according to my understanding of the term.
In my opinion they have more socialistic measures in force in Northern Ireland today than they have in any other country in the world that is not under a socialist government. As the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Gardiner) will be able to tell you, they have a rigid system of farm inspection and seed inspection for things like potatoes. They have a rigid system of inspection of those things which they export to the British market. In addition they have a socialized transport system. You can buy a ticket on the train and then use the other half to return by bus. I suggest to my Tory friends in this country that they wake up and study some of the measures that government has put into force.
Of course, as I say, it is not really a Tory government. Anybody who understands northern Ireland or southern Ireland knows what kind of government it is. You would never believe it to look at me now, but I was brought up to be a good Conservative and all my people were Conservatives. What they have there is really a unionist government; it is not a Tory government at all.

Transitional Measures Act I knew in the old country. Many of the things I saw were directly due to the system of controls and subsidies that was in force. I realize the necessity for state intervention in any system of private enterprise in order that the social rights of the individual within the state shall be protected and maintained.
We are dealing with a resolution respecting the continuation of certain controls. What those controls will be, we have merely an indication. Within the field of the control of prices, controls prevail over flour and bread, butter, sugar, cane molasses, imported fruits and canned vegetables. There is a further control over rentals, and there are also the specific controls requested by the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe) in respect of steel. Steel control was dealt with this afternoon in a very able and commendable manner by the hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Timmins).
So far as prices are concerned, the minister has made no statement indicating the degree to which controls will be maintained. The committee on prices, whose chairman was the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Martin), sat for three or four months last session and made recommendations which the government has not seen fit to put into effect at all. Following the adjournment of the meetings of that committee, a royal commission was set up. The commission has proven true to the record of many royal commissions in that, while it sat for a long period of time, its recommendations have not been acted upon. They must be of so little importance that we have not them before us at the present time, when the whole question of price control is being discussed. Indeed, the only hope we have of seeing this commission report is at the end of the present month when the printer has finally completed his task.
Royal commissions are set up for one of two purposes: first, to secure information upon which a decision may be made or, secondly, to evade responsibility for the making of any decision. Until we see the commission's report, each of us is left in a position of personally determining which of these two reasons prompted the setting up of that royal commission.
These control resolutions are based on the principle of the continuation of a national emergency. When the legislation was first introduced in the house in 1945, I remember well that it was generally understood the ministers of the crown expected the emergency arising out of the war would be of comparatively short duration. The government believes that we still have it with us although within the last year there has been a considerable reduction in the fields in which the government has been able to


infringe upon the jurisdictions of the provinces by means of the powers granted under the emergency controls.
An outstanding judgment in connection with emergency powers was delivered by the chief justice of the court of king's bench in Manitoba, in the case of Nolan v. Hallet and Carey, reported in 1948, (2) Dominion Law Reports, page 726. If I understand that judgment, it limits the sphere within which orders in council may be passed that purport to be passed under the powers contained in the emergency powers act.
Prices are at an all-time high and all the government has done has been to have a royal commission sit on the question, the report of which is still concealed in the hearts of the members of the government. We have the highest taxation in the history of this dominion and yet there is no apparent realization of the necessity of a substantial reduction in income tax rates to the end that there will be a greater incentive to producers and workers in the country. The Canadian dollar is at its lowest ebb in its history. In the international world, trade is disappearing at an accelerated pace, where our exports are being greatly reduced in our customary markets.
Oh, oh!

I am not referring to the United States; I am referring to our customary markets. As a result of the rigidity of bureaucratic controls, international trade finds itself jammed between controls brought into effect on foreign exchange and the controls on exports and imports. The world is in a condition of prohibitions, embargoes and quotas that determine whether there shall or shall not be trade. If ever there was a time when there should be an extra incentive for production, it is today.
Some of the members of the government may laugh, but throughout our country people are demanding, and demanding in tones that even this government should hear, that there must be a reduction in taxation. There is no excuse for the continuation of a system whereby, within the first nine months of the present fiscal year, the amount of excess taxation imposed by this government totals $610 million. On a per capita basis of population that means that, at a time when there should be an incentive, when there should be a further expansion on top of the expansion already taking place, $165 in unnecessary taxation has been extracted from every Canadian family within the last nine months.
At this very time when such a tremendous surplus is being built up the government is continuing to expend, and to expand controllable expenditure, at an unusual rate. The

facts are available as at January 15, 1949, in the issue of the Canada Gazette. It is set out there that the revenue and expenditure for the first nine months of 1948 starting April 1, 1948, resulted in a surplus of $609,949,000. It is also shown that within the same period controllable ordinary expenditures by government departments have increased by some $140 million, or at the rate of 48-9 per cent. If ever there was a time when the government, in the interests of the people as a whole, should be reducing its controllable expenditures, surely it is now. Do they say it cannot be done? I call as a witness Senator Crerar, a former member of this house and an experienced parliamentarian. Speaking on this question a few months ago he stated that, with fair application, and without in any way diminishing necessary services, the government of this country could reduce its controllable expenditures by $500 million. That is a statement by a statesman who sat in this house.
