I trust, Mr. Speaker, I shall speak with a bit more circumspection than the last speaker. I shall therefore leave St. Paul and all the rest of them out of it. The debate on this question has been generally related to the increased cost of living, and price control. Last year, the government appointed a special committee of this house to investigate the cause of the increase in prices and, allegedly, to try to find some cure for it. The reason for the appointment of this special committee was the fact that, at this time last year, prices were rising rapidly and had been doing so for some time. There was widespread alarm throughout the country on that account. The uproar was so great, the government felt compelled to do something to quieten it. As a result, the committee was appointed.
This committee was appointed, however, with power only to inquire and report back to the house. It did not have the power to recommend any action to the house. In other words, all the committee could do was to call witnesses, and it did call them for an interminable length of time. Eventually, the evidence ran to thousands of pages. For my sins I had to sit on that committee, and I became very tired of the futility of it. So far as I could see, it accomplished nothing. I now see, however, that it did accomplish one thing. It put on the record a great mass of evidence in connection with the reasons for the rise in prices during the past two or three years. It also put on the record a great deal of factual information as to the actual profits which producers, wholesalers, retailers and processors procured, particularly in connection with food products. As far as I can see, that is the only useful thing the committee did because it provides us at the present time with information which totally discredits the position taken by the C.C.F., and disproves many of their most-used arguments.
I regret as much as anyone the steep increase which has taken place in the cost of living. Particularly do I regret the hardships which, because of that fact, have been imposed upon people with small pension incomes; the so-called white-collar workers whose salaries, in a large number of cases, have not been increased to any great extent; the old age pensioners and the war pensioners
TMr. Williams.]

of one kind and another. Their plight has been rendered really desperate in many cases by the steep rise in the cost of living. It is discredited.

do that by attempting to sell to the country the idea that the rise in the cost of living has been chiefly due to the enormous profits secured by companies and businessmen across Canada.

Our price levels had to come up to them to some extent. The second reason was the increase in the amount of money in circulation. I should iike to say something about the constant cry of my socialist friends that controls should be reimposed to bring down prices. The evidence we had in the prices committee could be summarized by stating that this could not be done. The evidence was that the reimposition of controls could stabilize prices at their present level, and prevent their going higher; but it would not reduce them. It was not a practical proposition. It was stated, furthermore, that such an attempt to bring down prices by imposing over-all controls, or even controls to try to stabilize prices at present levels, was not workable in peacetime, that controls would need to be much more rigorous than they were during the war, and that they would lead to widespread black-markets and extraordinary difficulty in trying to maintain them. I have a good deal of evidence here in connection with that matter. I do not wish to take up the time of the house to read all of it. Q. This morning you made the observation that when controls were applied in 1941, that was postponing the trouble. Would you mind enlarging on that observation, please?
A. That is the way it necessarily turned out; and that, of course, could have been predicted at the time by anyone who foresaw that the war would last until 1945; but it was postponing it I believe to the great benefit of the public and of the war effort. To the extent that a runaway situation was averted during those years, I am sure that our war effort was much more effective than it could otherwise have been.
And again:
What I meant by saying postponing, was that price control did hold things so stable that we could not hope in a post war period to maintain that degree of perfection. There had to be some catching up with higher costs. And, of course, there often had to be a reflection of higher prices in other countries.

In the last annual report of the bank I have expressed this view (this will be found on page 20 of the report) :
"Short of substantially appreciating its exchange rate and increasing its taxation, no country could have insulated itself completely from the world-wide rise in prices. I should like to deal with the resolution before us more pointedly than I have in the general remarks I have been making. We are dealing only with the resolution and we do not know in what form the bill will be, but I presume it will be similar to the one last year and provide for the continuance of these powers.
Personally I would not be so much concerned if the things to be continued were stated specifically and with no power to add to them. I should like to see them limited to the commodities and services which were mentioned by the ministers, such as rent control, steel control, timber control, priorities control and price control on certain commodities.
Mr. Gar son: Where there are price ceilings.

I think we should get rid of some of these controls. I can see no reason why a ceiling should be maintained on butter.

Apparently the hon. member was following the evidence given last session in connection with butter. Has he noted that there has been no such profit this year as eleven cents per pound? Does he not admit that the present controls on butter have brought that condition about?
No, I do not admit that.

I do not know whether there is or not.
I am telling the hon. member.

Is the hon. member in favour of that?

Those people who prefer butter, and are willing to pay the price the farmer thinks he should get to cover his cost of production, may continue to buy it. I can see no logical reason for keeping butter under a price ceiling; it should be removed. The same thing applies to the rest of those foods still under price ceiling, such as bread, citrus fruits and other things. Personally I would be happy to see the price of citrus fruits go up two or three times so that the people of this country would drink apple juice, carrot juice and other things we have in this country, and thus help to eliminate some of the difficulties faced by the apple growers in Nova Scotia and other parts of Canada.
There is no reason for the continuation of these controls and I should like to see the government eliminate them. 1 do not think it is practical to get rid of rent control immediately. The government has managed to 29087-45 j

Until the present mess is cleared up I think we will have to have some measure of rent control. The same thing applies to steel control because of the shortages in that essential commodity.
I think the timber control might well go out the window. The lumber yards in Calgary appear to have an over-supply of lumber. There seems to be no shortage from what I can see and I do not think the continuation of this control is justified.

Mr. Speaker, I have listened to the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) with a great deal of interest. I do not know how the people in Calgary East feel about the controls that have been under discussion, but I do know how the people feel in the area which I represent. With all due respect to the hon. member for Calgary East, I venture to say to him that if the speech he has just delivered here in this House of Commons were delivered on a platform in my constituency he would certainly meet a very hostile audience. It may be that in my constituency there are not many packing-house owners or many lumber barons.
You must be very badly informed in your constituency.

Whether or not they are badly informed in my constituency, I think they are better informed than the hon. member for Calgary East. Those people have to use lumber. They are on the end when it comes to paying for the lumber. I am sure that young veterans returning from the last war, or munitions workers who saved their money and put it into government bonds in the hope that some day they would achieve the ambition of most Canadians, to own their own homes, when they came to buy lumber at present prices would be sufficiently disappointed. If they had to buy lumber without any price control they certainly would not like it in spite of the fact that in some parts of the country, perhaps in Calgary East, there may be a surplus of good lumber. There is no surplus in the place where the lumber originates, British Columbia. At the present time, I venture to say, the people of British Columbia will be most affected by the removal of the controls which this government proposes to carry on. I am dealing only with

Transitional Measures Act these controls, not with the innumerable controls which I should like to see the government institute on a number of things. Hon. members to my right may make the most of that, but I am simply dealing with the controls that the government proposes to continue.
The removal of those controls at the present time would affect certain classes of people in our country who are in desperate and straitened circumstances. It happens that they are centred in my constituency, because it is a place of rooming houses, and a large area is a place of slums. In these rooming houses, in the basement and in the attic, and in the slums, are the $40 a month burnt-out pensioners whom this country at one time treated as heroes. There are also the old age pensioners existing on $35 or $40 a month, people who gave the best that was in them to build the country and make possible the profits which my friends on the right consider to be reasonable and just. I suggest that this house represents them just as much as it does the lumber barons. Those are the people to whom we should have some sense of responsibility, and for whom these controls are essential.
I should like to point out that it was argued by the hon. member who spoke last that taxes, import duties, and the various tariffs that are placed on different things, are one of the essential causes for the maintenance of the present high prices. During the course of the discussion it was brought up as a matter of reproach that we should not look at things from the point of view of making as high a profit as we can. It was pointed out that we should not look at things from the point of view of buying in the cheapest market and selling in the dearest. It was pointed out that was essentially a philosophy which should not be followed. That statement was greeted with laughter on the right, and on the government benches. If that is the philosophy that is followed, and apparently it is, then if we remove all these taxes, if we remove all these tariffs, and if we make it possible for buying and selling to go on without the government taking any slice out of the amount for which the commodity finally sells, have we any reason to suppose that people will voluntarily bring down prices who believe they should make all the profit they can because when the next depression comes they may have to take a few losses?
Competition will do that.

Competition has not succeeded in doing that at any time. On the contrary, prices are determined at the present time, as was pointed out, by war produced shortages


where prices are uncontrolled, but wages are determined by the demand for labour. At the present time in my constituency, and in my part of the country, there are not less than
25.000	people drawing unemployment insurance. They certainly are not able to pay the prices which would result from the lifting of the existing controls. In addition to that, there must be at least half as many again who are unemployed but are not eligible to draw unemployment insurance. There are
7.000	between New Westminster and Abbotsford in the Fraser valley, as the member for Fraser Valley (Mr. Cruickshank) will tell you. In my section of the country at the present time fifty per cent of the industries have shut down because of the power shortage, resulting from a cataclysm of nature over which we have no control. These are the people whom I represent, and these are the people who would suffer if the policies advocated by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) were carried out.
I would say that by and large the people of the country are suffering from a reduction in the standard of living compared to that which they had a few years ago. It is pointed out in the speech from the throne, and the government has amply demonstrated, that we are going through a period of maximum prosperity. At the present time maximum prosperity, as it is regarded in orthodox free enterprise circles, is a period of maximum profits. At a time of maximum prosperity and maximum profits it is poor philosophy to rise on the floor of the house and demand that a reduction be made in the amoimt of taxes that industry has to pay. That section of labour power which has been incorporated in the commodity which we call surplus value, and for which the average wage worker receives nothing, is being cut into by the state, and big businessmen, and indeed some of the small businessmen are greatly annoyed about it.
But at the time of the hungry thirties, when there was no such surplus, when business was in a condition where many of the businessmen were facing bankruptcy, the type of controls that we have today were unnecessary. At the same time we are facing the prospect of a return to that sort of economic debacle unless we have some sort of planned society. These controls are a small step in that direction. It is at least a recognition by the state that they have some responsibility for the economic development of the country. They have some responsibility for maintaining the standard of living of the producers of the country. They have some responsibility for seeing that those citizens who have the weakest defences under a society of un-

limited competition, under a society in which there is no possibility of quarter being given, are protected, because they have no other protection.
I think that the policy of the government, while it is to that extent on the right track, should be carried further, that the existing powers that were given to the government by the house should be extended further. I believe that for this reason. I live in a section of Vancouver where I am three blocks from the industrial waterfront. I live in what is called a slum area, an industrial area. I, together with thousands of my fellow veterans, returned from overseas and I could not find accommodation. I had to live in an area where my standard of living, and the standard of living of thousands of other Canadian producers, has been cut away from under us, although we have always been led to believe that we had a right to the high North American standard of living.
Owing to the fact that prices make it impossible for us to build our own homes, we are compelled to live in a slum district. Two blocks away from where I live there is a house in which there are twelve adults and seven children. There is no bathroom and only one toilet. The chimney catches on fire regularly every month. The place was condemned years before the war. Yet we are compelled to utilize such accommodation simply because the existing price structure is getting in the way of expansion which is necessary to maintain a standard of living commensurate with the great wealth of the country. The contention has been made tonight that price controls could not continue in peacetime, that it would mean a police state. I ask hon. members whether they think that old age pensioners, burnt-out pensioners, and superannuated civil servants are bothered much about a police state provided they can keep prices within reach of their tiny means. By stigmatizing this progressive policy with the reactionary name of a police state, the critics are not going to alter anything in the minds of the people. The people feel this thing personally. They are not discussing it, as we are, in a theoretical atmosphere. Price controls mean something to them and are essential to them.
Great Britain has entered this discussion a considerable number of times today. I should like to say that Great Britain maintains a system of price controls. These controls had to be maintained because, unlike this country, the British people are not sitting on top of the world in so far as natural resources are concerned. There are perhaps forty to fifty million people concentrated in that tiny island. They have to import all their raw materials at high prices and then compete in
Transitional Measures Act the highly competitive markets- of the world with their finished products. The people of Britain have had to share and share alike. In that country, it is not possible for an extremely wealthy person to get what an extremely wealthy person can get in this country. It is possible, however, for poor children in that country to get all that is necessary to make for healthy bodies, much healthier than they were under the capitalist system. Together with this system of price control or perhaps because of this system of price control in Great Britain, the government is able to give the people security from the cradle to the grave; health insurance and old age pensions for women at sixty and men at sixty-five. Canada is one of the wealthiest nations per capita in the world, yet we are unable to afford those things because of the unlimited competition of capitalism and because of the irresponsibility of those who, at the present time, control our natural resources, our mines, mills and smelters.

I will permit a question later, but at the present time I am in full spate like the streams of British Columbia and I do not want to be interrupted.
Just like a phonograph.

It is no record to which you
are listening. In any event, the people like it and will continue to like it for some time. It will be heard more frequently on the floor of this house because the people like it. I would say that, so long as the prosperity, so called, continues at the existing level, there will be only discontent. The existing discontent has produced a protest to parliament in the form of the group of members I am amongst in this house. If the existing prosperity and the circumstances that go with it deteriorate, if they deteriorate only a little, we are going to experience in this country a tremendous change of heart.
The head of the welfare chest and the secretary of the red feather organization in the city of Vancouver, who is as far from being a socialist as my friend to the right, recently made this statement: that unless the federal authorities are willing to accept the responsibility for the mass unemployment which has developed there, and the lack of unemployment insurance to cover that situation, there will be serious riots and disturbances in that city. I have not been to Vancouver since early January, but this is the word of a man in a responsible position and drawing a salary equivalent to that of anyone in this house. He is a man whose business it is to know these things. Situations of that type are the

Transitional Measures Act direct consequence of the lack of control, the lack of planning, and unhampered competition.
At the present time the newspapers carry reports of very damaging floods in the south end of Vancouver island resulting in the loss of $100,000 worth of property. This flood is the direct consequence of the cutting-down of our trees in British Columbia without any thought of the necessity for replanting. In Sweden when one tree is cut down another is planted. They have been planting and cutting trees for hundreds of years. Owing to the lack of government controls in my province, in forty years we shall probably have no commercial timber within easy reach. We shall be going up to the top of the mountains for timber. Now, when the snow comes, it lies on the bare hillside and the first breath of warm weather brings flash floods. If the snow were shaded by the large trees, such floods would be avoided. At the present time the trans-continental trains are delayed twenty-four hours getting into the city of Vancouver. The same thing occurred last year on a tremendous scale, as this house knows.
I may sound rather radical to my hon. friends to the right and I may seem to have become somewhat emotional. I should like to say I have listened rather attentively to their point of view. I have not interrupted, nor do I intend to do so. I give my friends on the right credit for believing what they say, although I do not see how it is possible for them to believe all they have said. I do, however, give them credit for believing it. I know they believe it is their duty, but I should like them to have a look at this matter from the point of view of the man on the bottom of the pile. These controls are not being urged by the members of this group because we love controls. We love freedom as much as any man in this house. We do not want controls for the sake of controls. I do not want a policeman looking down the back of my neck or giving me a ticket every time I move. If it can be demonstrated, and I believe it can be, that in the interests of the country as a whole, during the transitional period from the production of war materials to the time when our peacetime production is again fully developed, controls are essential to the welfare of the majority of the people, then by all means let us use controls. Let us not look upon controls as a police state, but let us look upon controls as a means to an end and let that end be the best interests of the useful people of Canada.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner (Minister of Agriculture):
speechtext:
I do not know whether I can make the remarks which I hoped to be able to make by strictly adhering to the rules of the house. I think I can say all I wish to say,


however, by remaining as close to the rules as the other speakers have. The remarks which have just been made should, I think, have some reply. The hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Young) has covered considerable territory. I am sure he must have realized, as he was speaking, that a number of the subjects he was discussing were not of direct interest to the members of this house.
His reference to the control of the cutting of timber, for example, is a case in point. In this country the cutting of timber, if it is under the control of a government, is largely under the control of provincial governments. The natural resources, belong to the provinces and are, naturally, under their control. The only authority under which this government may take control over such matters is the type of authority we get from a measure such as the one under discussion this evening. I only wish to impress upon the hon. member the fact that we are being accused by the members of the official opposition now of trespassing upon provincial rights and we would probably be trespassing upon them still further if we attempted to do some of the things the hon. member has suggested.
I am very sorry I was not in the house this afternoon when the member for Peace River (Mr. Low) delivered his address. From what has been said, I would judge he had certain things to say with regard to conditions in the old land which he had recently visited. I have been in Britain on a number of occasions since 1936. I do want to agree with much of what has been said by the last speaker about the condition of the people and with much of what has been said by the member for Ontario (Mr. Williams). I am not prepared, however, to give all the credit to the present government in Great Britain for those conditions. *
Why?

My hon. friend says, Why? One of the reasons is that most of the social services referred to by the member for Ontario were placed upon the statute books of Great Britain by no less a person than one of his own very great countrymen, Lloyd George, a Welshman. That was many years ago, Mr. Speaker. It is true that other governments, Liberal, Conservative and Socialist, have added to the basic principles that were established by earlier governments. But when socialists attempt to take credit for all that was done by all social reformers back over the years, they are taking in much too much territory.
Then when I listen to the description of the condition of the people in London and in Britain at present, I am inclined to agree. But I should like to say to my hon. friend that the

members of the present government were calling my attention to those conditions during the first six months that they were in office. Anyone who knows the city of London realizes that conditions such as those that are being described could not have been created by any government in six months. The fact of the matter is that practically everything they have in Great Britain in the nature of controls of the distribution of food was placed upon their statute books and in the regulations by no less a person than Lord Woolton, the present chairman of the Conservative party in Great Britain and not a socialist at all. If any credit is coming to the present government in connection with those regulations and that legislation, it is due to the fact that they showed good enough sense under all the circumstances to continue the regulations which had been introduced under the Churchill government, and which are still in force.
May I say also that, in spite of the fact that much of the criticism has been made with regard to the controls they have in connection with agriculture, which might not be acceptable in the Dominion of Canada because of our different conditions, many of those controls also were not placed there under the present government. Some of them were introduced before the war and some of them early in the war during the period that Mr. Hudson was Minister of Agriculture in that country. I make these statements only for the purpose of keeping the record straight. In this country we have people who are trying to claim the credit for everything that has been done by anyone who has been interested in reform for a generation before there was a socialist party either in Great Britain or in Canada; and I think it is well that we should keep the record straight as to who is responsible for what, in order that we may be able to make decisions as to what we ought to do under certain circumstances.
Those were the days when Liberals were liberal.
Liberals are still liberal.
Not any more.

My friend Scotty, the hon. member for Selkirk, will be a Liberal some time in the future when he has made up his mind that he is no longer a socialist; because no Liberal ever desired to be controlled to the extent that the socialists want to control us. I have never known a Scotch Liberal who could stand for it for any great length of time.
Coming down to some of the discussions to which we have been listening, we on this side of the house have been the audience. We
Transitional Measures Act have been listening to a debate between the socialists and the Conservatives on the subject of controls. The socialists maintain that we ought to be controlled in every direction and with regard to everything we are doing.
They never said anything of the kind.
I am glad they are not quite as radical as they were a few months ago.
Keep the record straignt.

They too, or most of them, are coming back a little nearer to where they were at one time. Probably we shall find them doing as some of them used to do, organizing for one of the old parties. We shall probably find them even going to conventions and trying to get conventions for one of the old parties. Some of them, when they had tried on three or four occasions to get a convention for one of the old parties, and were not able to get it, then of course organized a party of their own and ran in order to try to get elected.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Page the hon. member for Springfield (Mr. Sinnott).

I realize that in order to get here they will have to do similar things, and probably some of them will be talking a little differently from the way in which they are now talking.
The argument that has been going on has been one as to whether we should or should not have controls; and again I say that we have been greatly interested in it. The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness), who is not here at the moment, had something to say with regard to butter, and I also want to say a little bit about it.
It is a fairly slippery subject.

Yes, it is a slippery subject. A certain party slipped out of power on it once, and the opposite party slipped out on another occasion. Someone might slip out again, but I do not think it will be this party.
Do not be too sure.

The question raised a few minutes ago with regard to butter is one that is well understood in this country. The farmers of Canada produce in the summertime twice as much butter as we consume, but in the winter months they produce half as much as we consume. As a result, speculators can have a good time with our butter if they are left free to do so. I rather imagine that some of those speculators would even be socialists who would be taking a chance on making a little bit out of butter.

Transitional Measures Act
Oh, no; surely not.

As a matter of fact, when you have twice as much of any product coming onto a market from which you cannot afford to let any of it go because you must have it all in order to supply the market completely throughout the year, if everyone is allowed to do what he likes about it, someone will do just what was done last year. The only reason such a great fuss was made about it last year was that it had not been done that way for seven or eight years. We had been at war, and the marketing of butter in this country had been under absolute control all the time. Then, when we let it out of control for a period, the butter was bought at under fifty cents a pound.
Just what we told the minister would happen actually did happen.

1 think I told my hon. friend it would happen. He might have agreed. It was bought at under fifty cents a pound. I think the evidence given to the committee was to the effect that even throughout the whole summer it was bought at an average of about fifty-one to fifty-two cents a pound. Then during the winter months, when there was coming onto the market only half enough to supply the requirements of the people, those who had in storage the butter which had been produced in the summer months were putting it on the market at a higher and higher price, until when it reached sixty-seven and one-half cents a ceiling was placed on it. That ceiling was the only thing that prevented it from going up higher. The only reason that the ceiling was put on was for the purpose of seeing to it that, since the butter had been bought at a lower price, it was not allowed to be sold to the people at any higher price than it had then reached.
When the matter was gone into by the committee it was found on the evidence that one of the companies had sold the butter at an average of between 11 cents and 12 cents a pound higher than it had been purchased, and of course everybody called that a profit. But what I want to emphasize is the fact that unless there is some kind of control some place that thing will happen in spite of what anybody tries to do every year from now on. The only reason that this government cannot do anything about it, unless a measure such as is before the house at the present time is passed, is that the authority to deal with that kind of thing is with the provinces. I am quite certain that if this government were to attempt to take that authority away from the provinces we would experience some of the same kind of criticism that this debate tMr. Girdiner.]

started off with this evening. The first speaker, the hon. member for Lake Centre (Mr. Diefenbaker), said, as I was coming into the chamber, that he was going to discuss certain orders from the point of view that they were encroaching, or allowing this government to encroach, upon the authority of the provinces. That has been quite an issue in almost everything that has been discussed this session, and I presume it is going to be made the issue by hook or by crook with regard to everything that is discussed from now until the end of the session.
What I should like to point out, Mr. Speaker, is that in so far as butter and many of these other products are concerned, there is now no effective control over them unless greater authority is given to the federal government than it has in relation to these matters up to the present time. The only reason that we were able to control butter during the war, the only reason that we have been able to control it last year, is that we had the War Measures Act during the war and we had the extension of the powers contained in the War Measures Act under the legislation which is under discussion at the present moment.
The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) was inclined to question my suggestion that the controls during this year made it impossible for those who have been handling butter to make as great a profit. Probably I was stating it the wrong way around. Probably what I should have said was that the controls, as they have been exercised this year, made it possible for men who have been trying for years to be honest in connection with this matter, and to trade with people honestly, to find a method of doing it under the controls as they are up to now. All that these controls did was to place a floor of 58 cents a pound under butter. That floor has not been operative at all during the past year in connection with the handling of butter because butter has never been down to that price or anywhere near it.
We had to import butter.

But having said that the ceiling price is approximately sixty-seven and a half cents-it differs a little from that in different places in Canada but that is the basis of it-may I say the fact is that all the butter has been bought at sixty-seven and a half cents. All the butter produced last May when there was twice as much coming on the market as was required, all the butter produced in June, all the butter produced right through the year, has been bought at approximately sixty-seven and a half cents a pound delivered at a certain point in Canada.

The regulation allows a certain margin, a certain markup, between that wholesale price and the retail price. With that certain markup between the wholesale price and the retail price-that markup is only a few cents; it does not permit of any profits to anyone of the kind that these people could make back over the years under the conditions that existed in this country-that narrow margin of markup has been all the profit that anyone could get. Therefore those who are storing the butter have been quite prepared to take delivery of butter, and pay the producer a certain price right through the year, whether in the summer or in the winter, for that butter. I think that every farmer in this country will say that sixty-seven and a half cents a pound is more money a pound for butter in the summer months than he needs to get in order to cover his costs of production. But I think every producer in this country will say that under present conditions sixty-seven and a half cents a pound for butter in the wintertime is not quite as much as he ought to get. But the two have averaged out at the best he has ever received in peacetime, possibly at any time.
Will the hon. member permit a question?
Yes.
Is it not a fact that milk which goes into butter yields a lesser return to the farmer than that which is used in any other form?
That is right, but it has not very much to do with what I am discussing at the moment.
It caused the sale of herds.

Perhaps the consumer ought to realize that the farmer is getting less money out of butter than he gets out of cheese, or out of canned milk, or out of whole milk sold at so much a quart each day; and as has been indicated, it is the lowest price. What I was trying to point out was that this year the farmer got approximately sixty-seven and a half cents a pound for his butter wholesale at, let us say, Montreal. The butter was then sold at a certain markup throughout the year, with the result that the man who was storing butter did not need to take all the risks that he used to take in connection with it and therefore did not need the margin. The risks are largely taken by the retailer who handles the butter. He may take delivery of it the day it is bought from the farmer, leave it in storage and take delivery of it from the wholesaler as he requires it for his customers.
Transitional Measures Act
I do not think there is an hon. member in this house-who fully understands the conditions under which butter is produced in this country, and fully understands the conditions under which butter must be marketed-who will not agree that some reasonable degree of control on the marketing of that butter ought to be put into effect and ought to be retained in effect. But I repeat, the only way that we can have that kind of control is by having some kind of understanding between this government and the provincial governments, which does not exist in a legal sense right up to the present time.
Is not that one of the best arguments which can be used for a Natural Products Marketing Act to co-ordinate the marketing agencies?

That may be so, but it is not
an argument for socialism.
I do not care what you call it.
It is one of the things which make people vote for socialism, because people who are not socialists do not regulate it, but it is not socialism.
Why are you not doing that?

We are doing it at the moment, and we are asking you to give us authority to do it for another year. That is all that is before this house at the moment. I am simply answering the suggestion of the hon. member for Calgary East who says that he does not want to give us that authority this year.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: Don't pay any attention to him.
I may not pay attention to him, but I pay attention to the people to whom he is talking when he speaks in this house.

Will the minister permit one question? In setting these prices for the handling of butter in the legitimate trade, is the minister getting complaints from these people or from those who want to speculate in butter?

So far as I know, we have not had any complaints from anybody this year. We have had no complaints from the farmers, from the retailers, from the wholesalers or from the consumers, except that some of the consumers who are probably not too well informed do not know what was suggested a few moments ago, namely, that our butter is being sold at the lowest price of anything that is made from milk.

And our herds in the eastern townships have been sold for the same reason.

Transitional Measures Act

I do not want to go into the discussion of that tonight. I am afraid my hon. friend will make me discuss it some other night when I come to my estimates. I merely wanted to deal with this one suggestion. On the one hand, people tell us that we must not step on the toes of the provinces, and on the other hand, occasionally by agreement with the provinces or in some other way, we find it absolutely necessary to do something which we have not the authority to do, in order to accomplish the things which people believe ought to be done in this country, no matter to what political party they belong.
It was not my intention to have taken up so much time in dealing with one product, butter. I had intended to spend more time in discussing the general position which has been discussed this evening. Our friends of the C.C.F. party have been maintaining, as they always do, that we should have retained all, or practically all the controls, and probably that we should have put on new ones that we did not have before. Then, our friends of the official opposition have been arguing that we have kept on too many controls up to now, and that we should have got rid of all of them, or at least the greater part of them.
You took the wrong ones off first.

I have an idea that out of the argument there has come a thought which perhaps did not occur to many of those who were speaking. My hon. friends of the C.C.F. party have been dwelling at great length upon the cost of living, and hon. members of the official opposition have occasionally drifted into that argument-that the cost of living is too high.
The hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) has tried to impress upon the house that food costs were possibly more responsible than anything else for increasing the cost of living; and hon. members in another part of the house argue that that is not so.
I should like to place on record one or two illustrations I have run across out in the country, to indicate the weakness of those arguments. Last summer while out in Saskatchewan I picked up a pamphlet which had on the back of it a big 59 in red numbers. Then, over the top of that was printed the inscription, "The purchasing power of the dollar today is only 59 cents". I looked at it, and then I said to the farmer I was visiting, "Do you agree with that?" "Well," he said, "it is not working out that way with me. I do not know just whom they are talking about. Perhaps they are taking an average all across Canada, and in that I do

not know whether they are right. But," he said, "in so far as I am concerned, I built a house this year; and the reason I built it was that I could build it with 34 per cent less wheat than I could have built it with before the war. I could have built it with 40 per cent fewer hogs than I could have built it with before the war. I could have built it with 56 per cent fewer cattle than I could have built it with before the war. So," he said, "my purchasing power in respect of those particular things today, with the dollar that I have, represented in products I have been selling, is away beyond what the pamphlet makes it out to be."
I think his reasoning was much sounder than the reasoning of some of my hon. friends who have spoken this evening.
Last summer out in the middle of Saskatchewan, where I did not think anyone knew me-
Oh, oh.
Where could that be?
-I walked into a restaurant. I will not tell you where it was.
Did you have to go there to eat?
I had intended only to have a dish of ice cream to cool me off.
Getting pretty hot?

The lady who was there ready to wait on me was seated at a table with a copy of the Winnipeg Free Press in front of her. She had not been reading the editorials they have been writing recently- but she was looking at the stock page. She called me by name and said, "Come over here, I want to show you something".
Oh, oh.

And she was not thinking about the same things as the hon. member for Ontario (Mr. Williams). When I went over and took a look at the paper it showed the picture of a big white steer, over which was the inscription, "The farmer got $546 for this one".
"Come up and see me some time".
I said to her, "That is a pretty nice steer". She said, "That was not what I was thinking about".
Oh, oh.

I said, "What were you thinking?" She said, "I was thinking that we could buy a tractor with three steers like that. I was just wondering how many it

would have taken in the years just before the war". That was an exceptional steer, it is true.
Exceptional woman, too.

Nevertheless, one could buy a tractor with six steers of the ordinary type. They would have brought just as much money as she would have had for three steers of the type of which she was speaking.
What I am hoping to do by these illustrations is to point out to the house that there is some truth in what was said by the hon. member for Calgary East, namely, that when we come to quoting percentages, quoting lump sums, and trying to apply our arguments to every condition that exists, no matter where we happen to be in different parts of this country, quite often we are talking with people who know a great deal more about their local conditions than we do. And I am afraid if my hon. friend the member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Young) goes around to some places and talks as he was talking a few moments ago he would find that in due course people would not be as well pleased as he thinks.
After all, most of the farmers in this country whom I have met-and I have met a great many of them-are thinking just as straight with respect to the economic problems of this country as are any group of people to be found anywhere. Most of them believe that they are enjoying as favourable economic conditions today as they have ever enjoyed at any time.
And they know why that is. Hon. members have been discussing the matter this evening. Someone over here said, "They cut out the subsidies"; and someone in another section of the house said, "They increased the cost of coarse grain," and so on. That is the kind of argument we have heard here, there and everywhere. Someone said, half under his breath, that at a particular time this was being done at the expense of the farmer; that in other words we did not let him have the highest possible price when prices were at their peak. And it is suggested that because we did not do that, we ought to throw our markets wide open now.
May I say to him that there are very few farm products which a farmer could sell in the United States market today at a better price than he is getting for them in the Canadian market-very few.
What about potatoes?
Butter.
Butter is higher in Canada.

Yes, butter is higher in
Canada. I look at the official prices every
29087-46i
Transitional Measures Act day, and I know the price has been down around 60 to 63 cents on comparable markets for some considerable time.
Not in whole milk?

Milk powder has been lower in the United States for about two years than it has been in this country. Than, cheese cannot be shipped from Canada into the United States, with freight and duty paid on it, and be sold at as high a price as it can be sold in Canada. That is why I am getting appeals every day from people all over this country who want us to take cheese off their hands, cheese that they have been holding for one or two years. This market is the best market they have at the present time, but it does not bring enough to cover all the carrying charges in addition to what was paid for it.
I repeat that there are not many farm products that can be sold on the open market outside of this country at prices better than can be obtained in the country at the present time. Anyone who stands up in this house and advocates a lower cost of living by reducing the cost of food products is trying to make it absolutely impossible for this government to carry out the undertakings which they gave back in 1944 to maintain for a time during the transitional period floors under the prices of farm products.
My hon. friends in the opposition say that we denied the farmers the top prices at a particular period. If you allow prices to go down to the level of prices in some markets in order to satisfy consumers all over the country, then the farmers will lose on the long-time experience.
1 think we have had enough men standing up in this house and saying that the farmer lost money on wheat because he did not get the top price, that we should have been on the open market all the time, and then advocating at the same time that we ought to make all farmers-there is only a small proportion, some 200,000 out of 750,000, who raise wheat-that we ought to make all the other 550,000 farmers and their families accept a lower return for their products simply because they cannot be sold at a higher price in some other place for the time being. That kind of argument is going to make it absolutely impossible to carry out even the kind of control that is necessary to stabilize prices for a limited period of time.
It was necessary during the war and after to hold down prices for farm products and other products, and prices were held down. If we are to have stabilized prices it may be necessary to hold up farm prices. My hon. friends of the C.C.F. say that because

Transitional Measures Act we have no ceiling price, therefore we have no control. They are not talking in accordance with the facts.
Never said that.

The hon. member says
"never said that". They said that controls have all been taken off farm products and not off other things.
It is the other way around.

Rather that controls have been taken off other things and not off farm products, with the result that farmers suffer. The keeping on of floors tends to keep up prices and for a period of time it tends to give the farmer back something of what he lost during the period when he was not allowed to take the peak prices he might have taken.
Let us examine for a moment or two the conditions and the time during which he did take comparatively low prices. The United States had controls right down to the end of the war and our people were not able to get much if any more, even if they had been able to get into the United States during that period. Shortly after the war the United States took off controls and prices rushed up very rapidly. Some people were inclined to say that we should have taken them off also and allowed our prices to run up just as rapidly. In other words we should have sold in the American market. Whether it was right or not, we did not do that; we maintained our prices at lower levels not only for food products but for labour and everything else. My hon. friend shakes his head. Probably there were a few things that one would buy once in twenty years or once in ten years that were higher.
Gasoline.

You can buy more gasoline with a bushel of wheat today than you could at any time over a long period. One hon. member said "What about rye?" I know this will not be an answer because I do not know where it came from.
Assiniboia.

If it came from the C.C.F. group it will not be an answer. If it came from the Social Credit group, it will be an answer. If it came from the Conservatives, it will be an answer. Some people have been saying that we should have kept the market open all the time, that there should have been a free market, that we should have let prices go where they would. Well, we did that with one product and I am going to tell the house why it was done because I was the culprit in the picture.


When controls were put on back in 1942 reasons were given for doing that. The first was that we wanted to keep down the cost of living in order that we could get more for the money that we were spending during the war period when we had to spend great sums of money to do the things that we would not do in ordinary times. It was thought that we should keep down wages in order to keep down the cost of production. We were working toward that end. With a few exceptions we controlled everything.
One thing we did was this. We did not tie the prices of food produced by the farmer to the price of the month period to which we tied almost everything else. We allowed the price of live hogs, we allowed the price of live cattle, and we allowed the price of grain to go up to higher levels before we put on absolute controls which resulted in those prices not going higher. Not only did we do that; we entered into contracts with Britain which took all our surplus at higher prices than we could have got in other places at that time. In other words, we improved the condition of the producers of food during that period.
That is one reason why the prices of food products were allowed to get up to a level which was much higher than the level at the time the prices of other products were fixed. Does anyone believe that the price of hogs did not go up between 1942 and 1945-46? Of course it did. Does anyone believe that the prices of farm products did not go up during that period? An effort was made by some people in this country-it was not the government-to tie wheat at the price it was selling for at that time, that is 78 cents. But the government did not permit wheat to be tied at 78 cents and it went up until it reached $1.25 before any particular effort was made to control it.
The only thing the government did during that period was to take wheat that nobody else would take. There was not an elevator company in this country, farmer, co-operative or otherwise, that would buy a bushel of wheat during the early forties at 50 cents. They all came to the government and said: "Take this wheat off our hands; put it in the elevators and allow us money with which to build annexes to our elevators so we can store it". The government did everything to make it possible for this product to be carried on to a later time in order to assist the farmers over a difficult period.
I think these things ought to be said when a discussion is going on of the kind that is going on here tonight. Those things were done. That is the reason why farmers will tell you when you drive into their yards that they are able to put up a building now with

less wheat than ever before. That is why they tell you that they are buying their gasoline, even at today's high price, for less bushels of wheat than they bought it before, or for less of the other farm products. These prices were not held at a dead level as of 1941. They were deliberately allowed to go up until they reached a higher level, and that higher level was maintained on products such as wheat right down to the end of the war. When wheat was sold at that price every single nickel was returned to the farmers with the result that the men who delivered during that period of time received another $60 million. We did not charge them the $60 million, Mr. Speaker, that we lost in the years just before that. We paid that out of the treasury.
When these people are figuring what has been lost and what has been gained they ought to go back to the beginning and figure the thing properly. If they figure it properly every one of them will come to the same conclusion that my friends have come to on rye. I got a letter from a man in Alberta the other day. He said, "I made a mistake. I put all my land in rye for the last three years, and I was hailed out for two of those years. This year it is down to less than $1 a bushel where I am." He hoped to get $4 a bushel for it when he put it in. That is what a so-called open market does for these fellows; that is what it does for them. Rye was around 50 cents a bushel when this thing started. Rye went right on up until it got to $4.30 a bushel. Farmers of the west put in rye against the advice of the government, against the advice of others. There was the offer staring them in the face; there was the propaganda from the grain exchange.
When I am on this question what I should like to say to my hon. friend from Souris (Mr. Ross) is this. I have heard him stand up in the house and say he is against the grain exchange.
It is not on the record.
I have heard him stand up in this house and say-
The hon. member for Springfield says that it was never on the record. I will show him in Hansard, where I moved a resolution. He is not making a true statement of fact.
It is on the record.
Can you give us the date?

He can get the date, and if he does not get it I will get it, because it is on the record.
Transitional Measures Act
The minister will correct you.

The record shows my hon. friend has been against the grain exchange. The record shows that my hon. friend is in favour of the wheat board. That is a logical position to take; but when I listened to him the other day, putting forward all the arguments that anyone ever put forth in support of the grain exchange, I began to wonder whether he was arguing for what he believes in, or whether he was arguing for something that somebody else believes in. If so, I should like to have his reason why he was arguing for something somebody else believes in. In so far as rye is concerned, rye started out below 50 cents a bushel at the beginning of the war and ran up to $4.30. It dropped from $4.30 down to $1.14 at Fort William, according to yesterday's paper. That is a very good illustration of what happened to wheat in the first war.
When we are able to say now what we are able to say in that regard I think we have something that is worth putting before the people of the country from time to time. To finish my story on rye, I said I was going to tell you that I was the culprit. Back in 1942, when the argument was on to keep down the cost of living, I said that rye was a crop which did not enter into the cost of living in this country. We do not eat rye bread, or very little of it. We do not convert it into flour. Even our chickens will not eat it. We only get our hogs to eat it because they do not have anything else. They do not like it. I said, "It is not used generally by farmers for feed and it is not used generally by human beings for food. The people who grow it live in the driest areas of western Canada where it is most difficult for them to grow anything, and if they can get a higher price for it at the present time it is not going to hurt anybody very much. It is not going to affect our cost of living, so let them have it."
I found that people who will take your advice when the price is going up refuse to take it when the price is going down. Last year I was saying to people not in the drought area, "Get out of rye. One of these days you are going to take an awful bump." Some of them did not get out, and they have learned now why an open market is not as good a thing as some people think it is. There is nothing of the nature of socialism in the fact that a man says that one system of marketing is better than another. That is not socialism. It is not socialism to be on

Transitional Measures Act either side of the question. The system which we have had for the last seven or eight years, whatever it may have done in the past and whatever it may do in the future, is the system that operated to the satisfaction of our producers all over western Canada. I am sure that unless they can be shown something better they will support it right through the years.
On motion of Mr. Hansell the debate was adjourned.
